say.text: Cairo, in the weeks of Shirkuh's vizierate. There is a table in the hall, and there is food on it.
Ibn Shaddad says that Shirkuh was a very hearty eater, so fond of rich dishes that he often suffered from surfeit and indigestion; after great pain he would recover.
The physician said you should leave the heavy dishes, uncle.
The physician has not run an army through a desert in a storm. A man who has done that is owed his dinner.
He is also owed an old age.
Hm. An old age. I have never seen one close. Sit down. Read to me from the treasury's accounts while I eat, and tell me where the money is.
Shirkuh entrusted the management of affairs to Salah ad-Din, on account of his great abilities.
It is in the hands of men who have no reason to give it to us. We shall have to be fair, uncle, or we will not be here a year.
That is my nephew. I never taught you that. You were born knowing it.
You taught me to count the bread.
So I did. Pass the dish.
